source_solutions.independent_solution: An electric field drives free electrons in a metal (or ions in an electrolyte) into directed motion. Their interactions with the constituent particles transfer electrical energy into internal energy and can warm the conductor. Current is not consumed, and charge carriers do not need to stop or accumulate to create heating. For the stationary purely resistive metal model, electrical work supplies the thermal energy; generated heat is not necessarily the conductor's own internal-energy increase because some energy may leave for the surroundings.
required_distinctions: Directed carrier motion and interaction with conductor particles.
Electrical energy becomes internal energy, not disappearing current.
Generated thermal energy and retained internal energy are different quantities.

source_solutions.independent_solution: For a stationary purely resistive conductor under constant U and I during t, A=UIt and all electrical work becomes thermal energy, so Q=A=UIt. Use volts, amperes and seconds to obtain joules. This equality concerns generated heat, including heat subsequently transferred out, not necessarily the conductor's retained energy. Do not extend Q=A to an electric motor's mechanical output or an electrolytic cell's chemical conversion.
required_distinctions: Purely resistive stationary scope.
Constant U and I over the measured interval.
Time in seconds for joules and heat/work equality within its scope.

source_solutions.independent_solution: Use Ohm's law U=IR in Q=UIt: Q=(IR)It=I^2Rt. For an entire interval represented by this product, I and R must be constant or approximately constant. The square comes from the original I multiplied by the I in IR. Recognition of this complete substitution chain can test derivation, but cannot show that a learner independently writes the algebra.
required_distinctions: Substitution of U rather than an unsupported memorized final expression.
Two current factors produce I squared.
Constancy assumptions for a finite-time product.

source_solutions.independent_solution: Joule-Lenz law in the model is Q=I^2Rt. Holding R and t fixed gives Q proportional to I^2, so multiplying I by k multiplies Q by k^2. Holding I and t fixed gives Q proportional to R. Holding I and R fixed gives Q proportional to t. These are controlled comparisons, not a claim that the higher-resistance element always heats more in every circuit. At fixed U and t in an ohmic purely resistive conductor, substitution I=U/R instead gives Q=U^2t/R, reversing the resistance comparison.
required_distinctions: Squared current dependence versus linear resistance and time dependence.
State which other quantities remain fixed in each comparison.
Fixed-current and fixed-voltage resistance comparisons are not interchangeable.

source_solutions.independent_solution: t=30 min=1800 s. With constant I=5 A and R=20 ohm, P=I^2R=25*20=500 W. Q=Pt=500*1800=900000 J=900 kJ. Equivalently U=IR=100 V and Q=UIt=100*5*1800=900000 J. Using 30 as seconds yields 15000 J; using I rather than I^2 yields 180000 J; multiplying by 60 twice yields 54000000 J.
required_distinctions: 30 minutes must be converted to 1800 seconds.
Current must be squared.
Heat units and power units must not be exchanged.

source_solutions.independent_solution: A secure low-resistance electrical contact reduces localized resistive heating and its associated overheating hazard; a loose or inadequately joined contact can have a large contact resistance. For the same through-current over the same duration, the junction's heat is I^2*R_contact*t, so lowering contact resistance lowers localized generated heat. This is not removal of all wire resistance or elimination of current. In a real supplied circuit changing contact resistance can also change I, so the controlled-current assumption must accompany a strict comparison. The source asks for the purpose and physical basis, not instructions to solder or dismantle a supply circuit.
required_distinctions: Contact resistance rather than conductor resistance everywhere.
Localized heating at a shared or comparable through-current.
Principle-only explanation; no energized repair activity.

source_solutions.independent_solution: Removing an energized immersion heater from water does not necessarily stop electrical heating. Heat removal becomes much less effective without surrounding water. If incoming electrical heating exceeds outgoing thermal transfer, the heater's internal energy and temperature rise and it may quickly fail. It is unnecessary and generally unjustified to assume the current grows or that the resistance falls upon removal; the decisive explanation is continued heat input with impaired cooling. The event is a fault analysis only, never an experiment to attempt.
required_distinctions: Electrical heat generation can continue outside the water.
Generated heat is not the same as retained energy.
Temperature follows net heat input, not heat generation alone.
No energized out-of-water experiment.

source_solutions.independent_solution: The three wires in series carry the same current and are energized for the same time, hence Q_copper:Q_steel:Q_cupronickel=R_copper:R_steel:R_cupronickel. For equal length L and cross-sectional area S, R=rho*L/S, so the heat ranking is the resistivity ranking under the stated comparison. For the usual classroom materials one expects cupronickel to have the highest resistivity and heat most, with ordinary steel above copper. However this seed provides no resistivity table, specified alloy compositions, temperature conditions or measured resistances, so that exact named-material ordering is an additional material-property premise, not deduced from the selected definitions alone. The fully seed-supported answer is conditional: the greatest resistance/resistivity produces the most heat at the common current and time. Teacher-led low-voltage demonstration can measure or compare heating safely; actually observing and explaining its evidence is a separate capacity from selecting an algebraic relation.
required_distinctions: Series implies equal current, not equal individual wire voltage.
Equal length and area make resistance proportional to material resistivity.
Specific material ordering requires material-property data or prior knowledge.
A teacher-led low-voltage verification task is not performed by a choice response.
source_solutions.input_limit: No seed-supported numerical resistivities or composition-independent proof of the exact material order. Preserve this limitation when judging coverage; do not invent data.
